title: Bridge Pattern
oneLiner: Splits an abstraction from its implementation so both can change independently, instead of multiplying subclasses.

hero.name: Crossover
hero.catchphrase: Change one side. The other doesn't even notice.
hero.power: Connects an abstraction to its implementation through composition, letting either evolve without touching the other.
hero.weakness: Sets up indirection before you need it — if the two sides never actually vary independently, Crossover is complexity with no payoff.
hero.origin: Crossover arrived after a shape-drawing library shipped `RedCircle`, `BlueCircle`, `RedSquare`, `BlueSquare` — a subclass explosion for every color/shape combination.

story.problem: A shape library models `Circle` and `Square`, then needs colors, so it creates `RedCircle`, `BlueCircle`, `RedSquare`, `BlueSquare`. Adding a third color or shape multiplies subclasses combinatorially.
story.solution: Crossover splits the hierarchy in two: shapes hold a reference to a `Color` implementation instead of inheriting from it. Shapes and colors now vary independently.
story.result: Adding a new color means one new Color class. Adding a new shape means one new Shape class. No combinatorial explosion, ever.

before: Adding a color multiplies the subclass count
Shape logic and color logic are tangled together
after: Shapes and colors are separate, independently-varying hierarchies
Adding a color or shape means exactly one new class
Shape logic and color logic stay cleanly separated

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A class diagram shows RedCircle, BlueCircle, GreenCircle, RedSquare, BlueSquare, GreenSquare — and a third shape is coming.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We need a Triangle now. That's three MORE subclasses. This is multiplying out of control.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Crossover appears, standing exactly between two separate towers: Shapes and Colors.
panels.speaker: Crossover
panels.dialogue: Stop inheriting color into shape. Give shape a REFERENCE to a color instead — then they can grow separately.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Shape holds a Color implementation. Circle and Square each just call color.fill().
panels.speaker: Crossover
panels.dialogue: Any shape can use any color, with zero new classes for the combination itself. Just plug one implementation into another.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Triangle ships with one new class. It instantly works with every existing color.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One Triangle class, and it already supports red, blue, and green. No combinatorial mess.

useWhen: You have two dimensions of variation (shape/color, device/OS, control/renderer) that would otherwise multiply subclasses.
You want to swap out an implementation at runtime without touching the abstraction that uses it.
Both the abstraction and its implementation are expected to grow independently over time.
avoidWhen: There's really only one dimension of variation — a normal inheritance hierarchy is simpler.
The two 'sides' will never actually vary independently in practice — the split adds ceremony for nothing.
The codebase is small enough that a future refactor to Bridge would be cheap if the need ever arises.
commonMistakes: Introducing Bridge preemptively for a single dimension of variation that doesn't need it yet.
Confusing Bridge with Adapter — Bridge is designed upfront to let two sides vary together; Adapter retrofits compatibility after the fact.
Letting the abstraction leak implementation details, defeating the point of separating the two hierarchies.
Not documenting which side is the 'abstraction' and which is the 'implementation', confusing future contributors.
explanation.realWorldExample: JDBC/ODBC (a single Connection abstraction over many database driver implementations), cross-platform UI toolkits separating widget abstraction from OS-specific rendering, and device drivers separating a common API from vendor-specific implementations all use Bridge.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: This looks a lot like Strategy — swapping an implementation behind an interface.

conversation.speaker: Crossover
conversation.message: Structurally similar, different intent. Strategy swaps ONE algorithm at a time for ONE class. I split a whole hierarchy in two so BOTH sides can grow independently, long-term.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So I shouldn't reach for you on day one?

conversation.speaker: Crossover
conversation.message: Right — that's my weakness. Wait until the subclass explosion actually starts, then split the hierarchy. Premature splitting is just extra indirection.

codeBattle.scenario: Your remote-control app needs to support 3 device types (TV, Radio, Speaker) and 2 remote styles (Basic, Advanced), and both lists are expected to keep growing.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Crossover splits Remote (abstraction) from Device (implementation) so new remote styles and new device types can each be added independently, without multiplying subclasses.

quiz.question: What core problem does Bridge solve?
options: Two independent dimensions of variation cause a combinatorial explosion of subclasses
An object needs to notify many listeners of a state change
A single instance needs to be shared globally
An interface needs a simplified entry point
quiz.answer: Two independent dimensions of variation cause a combinatorial explosion of subclasses
quiz.explanation: Bridge exists specifically to split two independently-varying hierarchies apart via composition instead of inheritance.

quiz.question: How does Bridge separate abstraction from implementation?
options: The abstraction holds a reference to an implementation interface instead of inheriting from it
It deletes the implementation entirely and hardcodes behavior
It merges abstraction and implementation into one class
It requires a database to store the implementation
quiz.answer: The abstraction holds a reference to an implementation interface instead of inheriting from it
quiz.explanation: Composition over inheritance is exactly how the two sides become free to vary independently.

quiz.question: When is introducing Bridge premature?
options: When there's only one dimension of variation and no combinatorial explosion is happening
When you already have four shape types and four color types
When both the abstraction and implementation change frequently
When you need to swap implementations at runtime
quiz.answer: When there's only one dimension of variation and no combinatorial explosion is happening
quiz.explanation: Bridge's cost (an extra layer of indirection) only pays off once two dimensions are genuinely multiplying subclasses.

quiz.question: How does Bridge differ from Strategy?
options: Bridge structurally splits a whole hierarchy in two; Strategy swaps one algorithm for a single class at a time
They are identical patterns with different names
Strategy requires inheritance, Bridge forbids it
Bridge can only be used with UI code
quiz.answer: Bridge structurally splits a whole hierarchy in two; Strategy swaps one algorithm for a single class at a time
quiz.explanation: Bridge is a structural, long-term hierarchy split; Strategy is a narrower, single-class behavioral swap.
